blocks.body:
The integers, the polynomials with real coefficients, the $2 \times 2$ matrices and the residues modulo $n$ can all be added, subtracted and multiplied, and the familiar laws such as distributivity hold in each. A ring is anything with this structure. Seen this way, constructions that look different are one construction: building $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ from $\mathbb Z$, building the complex numbers from real polynomials, and building finite fields from polynomials over $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ are all quotient rings.

The subsets one can divide out by are called ideals, and properties of the ideal decide what kind of ring the quotient is. This lesson is the bridge from [[congruences]] to field theory; from [[groups]] it uses only the definitions of a group and a subgroup.

blocks.title: Ring
blocks.body:
A ring is a set $R$ with two operations $+$ and $\cdot$ and two elements $0$ and $1$ such that $(R, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$, multiplication is associative with identity $1$, and the distributive laws $a(b + c) = ab + ac$ and $(a + b)c = ac + bc$ hold. The ring is commutative if $ab = ba$ for all $a, b$.

In a commutative ring $R$: a unit is an element with a multiplicative inverse; a zero divisor is an element $a \ne 0$ such that $ab = 0$ for some $b \ne 0$; $R$ is an integral domain if $1 \ne 0$ and $R$ has no zero divisors; and $R$ is a field if $1 \ne 0$ and every nonzero element is a unit.

So a ring is a place where one can add, subtract and multiply, and in a field one can also divide by anything nonzero.

blocks.title: A gallery of rings
blocks.body:
- $\mathbb Z$ is an integral domain whose only units are $\pm 1$; $\mathbb Q$, $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$ are fields.
- $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is a commutative ring. The class of $a$ is a unit exactly when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$ ([[mod-inverse]]), and every other nonzero class is a zero divisor: if $d = \gcd(a, n) > 1$ then $a \cdot (n/d) \equiv 0$ although $n/d \not\equiv 0$. So $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is a field when $n$ is prime and has zero divisors when $n > 1$ is composite. Modulo $12$ the units are $1, 5, 7, 11$.
- If $R$ is commutative, $R[x]$ is the ring of polynomials with coefficients in $R$. If $R$ is an integral domain, so is $R[x]$, and $\deg(fg) = \deg f + \deg g$ for nonzero $f, g$, because the product of the leading coefficients is nonzero.
- The Gaussian integers $\mathbb Z[i] = \{a + bi : a, b \in \mathbb Z\}$ form an integral domain, being a subring of $\mathbb C$ ([[gaussian-integers]]).
- The real $2 \times 2$ matrices form a non-commutative ring with zero divisors:
$$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$

From now on rings are commutative. A few rules hold in every ring and are worth deriving once: $0 \cdot a = 0$, from $0a = (0 + 0)a = 0a + 0a$; and $(-1)a = -a$, from $a + (-1)a = (1 + (-1))a = 0a = 0$. In an integral domain one may cancel: if $ab = ac$ and $a \ne 0$, then $a(b - c) = 0$ forces $b = c$.

blocks.title: Ring homomorphism and ideal
blocks.body:
A ring homomorphism is a map $\varphi : R \to S$ with $\varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b)$, $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$ and $\varphi(1) = 1$. Its kernel is $\ker\varphi = \{a \in R : \varphi(a) = 0\}$.

An ideal of $R$ is a subset $I$ that is a subgroup of $(R, +)$ and absorbs multiplication:
$$a \in I,\ r \in R \implies ra \in I.$$
For $a \in R$, the set $(a) = \{ra : r \in R\}$ is the principal ideal generated by $a$; more generally $(a_1, \dots, a_k) = \{r_1 a_1 + \dots + r_k a_k : r_i \in R\}$.

Ideals play the role for rings that normal subgroups play for groups. Every kernel is an ideal: if $\varphi(a) = 0$ then $\varphi(ra) = \varphi(r) \cdot 0 = 0$.

blocks.title: Quotient rings
blocks.body:
Given an ideal $I$, write $a \equiv b \pmod I$ when $a - b \in I$. For $R = \mathbb Z$ and $I = n\mathbb Z$ this is ordinary congruence modulo $n$. The classes $a + I = \{a + i : i \in I\}$ form a set $R/I$, and we define
$$(a + I) + (b + I) = (a + b) + I, \qquad (a + I)(b + I) = ab + I.$$
To see that the answers do not depend on the chosen representatives, suppose $a' = a + i$ and $b' = b + j$ with $i, j \in I$. Then $a' + b' = (a + b) + (i + j)$ with $i + j \in I$, and
$$a'b' = ab + (aj + ib + ij),$$
where the bracket lies in $I$ precisely because $I$ absorbs multiplication. So both operations are well defined. The ring axioms for $R/I$ are inherited from $R$, with zero $0 + I = I$ and identity $1 + I$, and $a \mapsto a + I$ is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $I$. So, as for groups, ideals are exactly the kernels of ring homomorphisms.

blocks.title: First isomorphism theorem for rings
blocks.body:
If $\varphi : R \to S$ is a ring homomorphism, then $\ker\varphi$ is an ideal of $R$, $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ is a subring of $S$, and
$$R/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi \quad \text{via} \quad a + \ker\varphi \mapsto \varphi(a).$$

We saw that the kernel is an ideal; the image contains $1$ and is closed under the operations. Write $K = \ker\varphi$. Since $\varphi$ respects subtraction, $\varphi(a) = \varphi(b)$ if and only if $\varphi(a - b) = 0$, that is $a - b \in K$, that is $a + K = b + K$. Read from right to left, this says that $\bar\varphi(a + K) = \varphi(a)$ is well defined; read from left to right, that $\bar\varphi$ is injective. It maps onto $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ by construction, and it respects the operations because $\varphi$ does: $\bar\varphi(ab + K) = \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, similarly for sums, and $\bar\varphi(1 + K) = 1$.

blocks.title: Ideals of Z and of K[x]
blocks.body:
In $\mathbb Z$ every ideal is principal. Let $I \ne \{0\}$ be an ideal and $n$ its smallest positive element (if $a \in I$ then $-a \in I$, so positive elements exist). For $a \in I$ divide: $a = qn + r$ with $0 \le r < n$. Then $r = a - qn \in I$, so $r = 0$ by the choice of $n$, and $I = n\mathbb Z$. The same argument with polynomial division shows that if $K$ is a field, every nonzero ideal of $K[x]$ is generated by any of its nonzero elements of smallest degree. An integral domain in which every ideal is principal is called a principal ideal domain.

Ideals turn statements about numbers into statements about sets. In $\mathbb Z$, $(a) \subseteq (b)$ means $b \mid a$. The ideal $(a, b) = \{ax + by : x, y \in \mathbb Z\}$ is principal, and its generator is $\gcd(a, b)$; this is [[bezout]]. And $(a) \cap (b) = (\operatorname{lcm}(a, b))$. For example $(12, 18) = (6)$ and $(12) \cap (18) = (36)$.

blocks.title: Maximal and prime ideals
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $I \ne R$ an ideal. Call $I$ maximal if the only ideals containing $I$ are $I$ and $R$, and prime if $ab \in I$ implies $a \in I$ or $b \in I$. Then

1. $R/I$ is a field if and only if $I$ is maximal;
2. $R/I$ is an integral domain if and only if $I$ is prime.

In particular every maximal ideal is prime.

In both parts $1 + I \ne 0 + I$, because $1 \notin I$ (an ideal containing $1$ contains every $r = r \cdot 1$, and $I \ne R$).

1. Suppose $I$ is maximal and $a \notin I$. The set $J = \{i + ra : i \in I,\ r \in R\}$ is an ideal containing $I$ and $a$, so $J \ne I$, and by maximality $J = R$. Thus $1 = i + ra$ for some $i \in I$, $r \in R$, which says $(r + I)(a + I) = 1 + I$: every nonzero class is invertible, and $R/I$ is a field. Conversely, suppose $R/I$ is a field and $J \supsetneq I$ is an ideal. Pick $a \in J \setminus I$. Then $a + I$ has an inverse $r + I$, so $ra - 1 \in I \subseteq J$. Since $ra \in J$, also $1 = ra - (ra - 1) \in J$, and $J = R$. So $I$ is maximal.

2. In $R/I$, the product $(a + I)(b + I)$ is zero exactly when $ab \in I$, and $a + I$ is zero exactly when $a \in I$. So "$R/I$ has no zero divisors" is literally the statement "$ab \in I$ implies $a \in I$ or $b \in I$".

Since a field is an integral domain, maximal ideals are prime.

blocks.title: Building the complex numbers
blocks.solution:
Let $\varphi : \mathbb R[x] \to \mathbb C$ be evaluation at $i$, $\varphi(f) = f(i)$. Substituting a number into polynomials respects sums and products, so $\varphi$ is a ring homomorphism, and it is onto because $\varphi(a + bx) = a + bi$.

The kernel contains $x^2 + 1$, hence the whole ideal $(x^2 + 1)$. Conversely, suppose $f(i) = 0$. Divide by $x^2 + 1$: $f = q \cdot (x^2 + 1) + (a + bx)$ with $a, b \in \mathbb R$. Evaluating at $i$ gives $0 = a + bi$, so $a = b = 0$ and $f \in (x^2 + 1)$. Thus $\ker\varphi = (x^2 + 1)$, and the first isomorphism theorem gives $\mathbb R[x]/(x^2 + 1) \cong \mathbb C$.

In the quotient the class of $x$ satisfies $x^2 \equiv -1$: it is a square root of $-1$. This construction produces $\mathbb C$ without assuming in advance that it exists. Since the quotient is a field, $(x^2 + 1)$ is a maximal ideal of $\mathbb R[x]$.

blocks.title: A quotient of the Gaussian integers
blocks.body: Show that $\mathbb Z[i]/(2 + i) \cong \mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$.
blocks.solution:
Modulo $2 + i$ we have $i \equiv -2$, which suggests the map $\varphi(a + bi) = (a - 2b) \bmod 5$. It respects addition. For products,
$$(a + bi)(c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i \ \mapsto\ ac - bd - 2ad - 2bc,$$
while $(a - 2b)(c - 2d) = ac - 2ad - 2bc + 4bd \equiv ac - 2ad - 2bc - bd \pmod 5$. These agree, $\varphi(1) = 1$, and $\varphi$ is onto because $\varphi(a) = a \bmod 5$.

Since $\varphi(2 + i) = 2 - 2 = 0$, the kernel contains $(2 + i)$. Conversely, suppose $a \equiv 2b \pmod 5$. Then
$$\frac{a + bi}{2 + i} = \frac{(a + bi)(2 - i)}{5} = \frac{(2a + b) + (2b - a)i}{5},$$
and $2b - a \equiv 0$, $2a + b \equiv 4b + b \equiv 0 \pmod 5$. So the quotient is a Gaussian integer and $a + bi \in (2 + i)$. Hence $\ker\varphi = (2 + i)$ and $\mathbb Z[i]/(2 + i) \cong \mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$.

The quotient is a field, so $(2 + i)$ is maximal: $2 + i$ is a prime of $\mathbb Z[i]$, one of the two factors in $5 = (2 + i)(2 - i)$ (compare [[sums-of-squares]]).

blocks.title: Idempotents modulo n
blocks.body: Let $n = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_k^{e_k}$ with distinct primes $p_i$. How many $x \in \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ satisfy $x^2 \equiv x \pmod n$?
blocks.solution:
For rings $R$ and $S$, the product $R \times S$ is the ring of pairs with componentwise operations. The map
$$\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z \to \mathbb Z/p_1^{e_1}\mathbb Z \times \cdots \times \mathbb Z/p_k^{e_k}\mathbb Z, \qquad x \mapsto (x \bmod p_1^{e_1}, \dots, x \bmod p_k^{e_k})$$
respects sums and products, and by the [[crt]] it is a bijection; so it is a ring isomorphism. An equation such as $x^2 = x$ therefore holds in $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ exactly when it holds in every component, and the solutions modulo $n$ correspond to choices of a solution modulo each $p_i^{e_i}$.

Modulo a prime power $p^e$, the condition $p^e \mid x(x - 1)$ is easy to solve. The numbers $x$ and $x - 1$ are coprime, so $p$ divides at most one of them, and then $p^e$ divides that one: $x \equiv 0$ or $x \equiv 1 \pmod{p^e}$. Two solutions per prime power give $2^k$ solutions modulo $n$.

For $n = 60 = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ there are $8$: $0, 1, 16, 21, 25, 36, 40, 45$. For instance $16 \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, $16 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, $16 \equiv 1 \pmod 5$, and $16^2 = 256 = 4 \cdot 60 + 16$. Elements $e$ with $e^2 = e$ are called idempotents; one other than $0$ and $1$ always signals that a commutative ring splits as a product of two rings.

blocks.body:
- An ideal is not the same as a subring. $\mathbb Z$ is a subring of $\mathbb Q$ but not an ideal, since $\frac12 \cdot 1 \notin \mathbb Z$. An ideal containing $1$, or any unit, is the whole ring.
- Not every ideal is principal. In $\mathbb Z[x]$ the ideal $(2, x)$ consists of the polynomials with even constant term. A generator $g$ would divide both $2$ and $x$, forcing $g = \pm 1$; but $1 \notin (2, x)$.
- Cancellation needs an integral domain: in $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$, $2 \cdot 3 = 2 \cdot 0$ although $3 \ne 0$.
- With zero divisors, a polynomial can have more roots than its degree: $x^2 - 1$ has the four roots $1, 3, 5, 7$ in $\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z$. The bound "at most $\deg f$ roots" holds over integral domains.
- In a non-commutative ring, an ideal must absorb multiplication on both sides ($ra$ and $ar$) for $R/I$ to be a ring.

Quotients $K[x]/(f)$ by irreducible polynomials build new fields ([[fields-ext]]), and with $K = \mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ they build all [[finite-fields]]. In rings of algebraic integers such as $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, factorisation of elements is not unique ($6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})$), and Dedekind's repair is to factor ideals instead ([[ideals]], [[class-group]]). The [[crt]] is the ring isomorphism $\mathbb Z/mn\mathbb Z \cong \mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ for coprime $m, n$, and the roots of a polynomial over $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ can be counted prime power by prime power, as in the idempotent example and in [[hensel]].

1. List the units and the zero divisors of $\mathbb Z/18\mathbb Z$.
2. Show that $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2 - 2) \cong \{a + b\sqrt 2 : a, b \in \mathbb Q\}$.
3. Show that $\mathbb R[x]/(x^2 - 1)$ is not an integral domain, and find an isomorphism between it and $\mathbb R \times \mathbb R$.
4. Show that the ideal $(x)$ of $\mathbb Z[x]$ is prime but not maximal.
